It is interposed between them with this clause, and the meaning is: among the hardships is that one like you, despite the great sanctity of this city, is made lawful in it, just as game is made lawful outside the sanctuary (*ḥaram*).

Al-Wahidi said: *al-ḥill*, *al-ḥalāl* and *al-maḥall* are one and the same; it is the opposite of the forbidden (*al-muḥarram*). God made Mecca lawful for His Prophet ﷺ on the day of the Conquest until he fought in it, and the Prophet ﷺ had said: "It was not made lawful for anyone before me, nor will it be made lawful for anyone after me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day." He said: The meaning is that when God mentioned the oath by Mecca, this indicated the greatness of its status despite its being sacred, so He promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would make it lawful for him so that he would fight in it and conquer it at his hand. This is a promise from God, the Exalted, that He would make it lawful for him so that it would be lawful for him. End of quotation.

So the meaning is: "and you are a lawful resident in this city in the future," as in His saying: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30]. Mujahid said: the meaning is, whatever you do in it, you are lawful (*fa-anta ḥill*).

Qatadah said: "You are lawful in it" means you are not sinful: that is, you do not commit in this city what is forbidden for you to commit, unlike the polytheists who commit disbelief and sins in it.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "I do not swear by this city" while you are residing in it and it is your dwelling place. According to the view that "*lā*" is a negation and not superfluous, the meaning is: I do not swear by it while you are residing in it, so you are more worthy of the oath by you. According to the view that it is superfluous, the meaning is: I swear by this city in which you reside, as an honour for you and an exaltation of your rank, because by your residence in it, it has become great and noble, and has increased in the nobility and greatness it already had. However, this is established in the language of the Arabs: the word *ḥill* comes in the sense of *ḥāll* (resident). And just as the clause may be parenthetical, it may also be in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). ﴿And begetter and what he begot﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to "the city."

Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: ﴿and begetter﴾ means Adam, ﴿and what he begot﴾ means whatever was propagated from his offspring. He swore by them because they are the most wondrous of what God created on the face of the earth, due to what is in them of eloquence, intellect and management, and among them are the prophets, scholars and righteous.

Abu ʿImran al-Jawni said: the begetter is Abraham, and "what he begot" is his descendants.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "*mā*" is an expression for people, like His saying: ﴿what seems good to you﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 3]. It has been said: the begetter is Abraham, and the begotten is Ishmael and Muhammad ﷺ.

ʿIkrimah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: ﴿and begetter﴾ means the one who fathers (*alladhī yūlad lahu*), and ﴿and what he begot﴾ means the barren one who does not beget. It seems that these two took "*mā*" as a negation, and this is far-fetched; it is only valid by supposing an omitted relative pronoun: that is, "and the begetter and the one who did not beget," and the omission of a relative pronoun is not permitted according to the Basrans.

ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi said: it is general for every begetter and begotten among all animals, and Ibn Jarir chose this view.

﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾: this is the answer to the oath. "Man" (*al-insān*) is this human species. "*Al-kabad*" is hardship and difficulty. It is said: "*kābadtu al-amr*" (I struggled with the matter): I endured its hardship. Man continues to struggle with this world and endure its hardships until he dies. The root meaning of *kabad* is hardship, and from it comes "*takabbada al-laban*" (the milk thickened and became firm) when it becomes thick and firm. It is also said "*kabida al-rajul*" when his liver was afflicted, then it came to be used for every hardship and difficulty. From it is the saying of Abu al-Asbagh:

"I have a cousin who, if all people were in toil, would remain confined by arrows, shooting at me."

Al-Hasan said: he struggles with the calamities of this world and the hardships of the Hereafter.

He also said: he struggles with gratitude in times of ease, and he struggles with patience in times of hardship; he is never free of one of them.

Al-Kalbi said: this verse was revealed concerning a man of the Banu Jumah called Abu al-Ashaddayn, who used to take a leather hide of ʿUkaz and place it under his feet, saying: "Whoever removes me from it, for him is such-and-such." Ten men would pull it until it tore, yet his feet would not move. He was one of the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ, and concerning him was revealed ﴿Does he suppose that no one will have power over him﴾, meaning because of his strength. On this view, the meaning of ﴿in toil﴾ is: in the hardness of creation. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿in toil﴾ is that he is bold of heart and hard of liver. ﴿Does he suppose that no one will have power over him﴾: that is, does the son of Adam suppose that no one will have power over him and no one will take vengeance upon him? Or does Abu al-Ashaddayn suppose that no one will have power over him? "*Anna*" here is the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, and its noun is an implied pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr shaʾn*).

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the speech of this man, and said: ﴿He says: I have squandered abundant wealth﴾, that is, much accumulated wealth, some of it piled upon some.

Al-Layth said: *mālun lubad* is wealth whose ending is not feared because of its abundance.

[p. 1624]

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: he says, "I have squandered much wealth in hostility to Muhammad."

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal, who committed a sin and sought a ruling from the Prophet ﷺ, and he ordered him to make expiation, and he said: "My wealth has gone in expiations and expenditures since I entered the religion of Muhammad."

Al-Jumhur read *lubbadan* with a damma on the lam, a fatha on the ba, and shadda.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: *lubad* is on the pattern *fuʿal* from *al-talbīd* (layering), which is abundant wealth piled upon itself.

Al-Zajjaj said: *fuʿal* indicates abundance; it is said "*rajulun ḥuṭam*" when he is one who breaks much.

Al-Farrāʾ said: its singular is *lubadah* and the plural is *lubad*.

The explanation of this has already passed in the surah of the Jinn.

﴿Does he suppose that no one has seen him?﴾ That is, does he suppose that no one has witnessed him? Qatadah said: Does he suppose that God, glorified is He, has not seen him, and will not ask him about his wealth, from where he earned it and where he spent it? Al-Kalbi said: he was lying, he did not spend what he claimed; so God said: Does he suppose that God did not see that from him, whether he did it or did not do it, whether he spent or did not spend?

Then He mentioned what He had bestowed upon them, so that they might take heed, and said: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes﴾, with which he sees.

And a tongue with which he speaks, and two lips with which he covers his mouth.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: did We not do to him what indicates that God is capable of resurrecting him? The *shafah* (lip) has a missing *lām*, and its original form is *shafahah*, as evidenced by its diminutive *shufayhah*.

﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾. *Al-najd* is the road in an elevated place.

The exegetes said: We made clear to him the path of good and the path of evil.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Did We not make him know the path of good and the path of evil, both made clear, like the two high roads being clear?

ʿIkrimah, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak said: *al-najdān* are the two breasts, because they are like the two paths for the life and sustenance of the child. The first view is preferable.

The root meaning of *najd* is an elevated place, its plural is *nujūd*, and from it Najd was named because of its elevation above the lowland of Tihamah. So *al-najdān* are the two high roads. From it is the saying of Imru al-Qays:

"A group of them cut through the valley of Nakhlah, and another group of them cut through the highland of Kabkab."

﴿But he did not attempt the steep path﴾. *Al-iqtiḥām* is throwing oneself into something without deliberation. It is said from it: "*qaḥama fī al-amr quḥūman*," that is, he threw himself into it without deliberation. And "*taqḥīm al-nafs fī al-shayʾ*" is putting oneself into it without deliberation. *Al-quḥmah* with a damma is ruin.

*Al-ʿaqabah* originally means the road in a mountain, named so because of the difficulty of traversing it. It is a parable that God, glorified is He, struck for striving against the self, desire and Satan in works of righteousness, making him like one who laboriously climbs the steep path.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjaj said: God mentioned here "*lā*" only once, and the Arabs hardly ever use "*lā*" alone with the past verb in such a position unless they repeat it in another utterance, as in His saying: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31]. He used it singly here to indicate the meaning through the end of the speech. So His saying ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ may stand in place of repetition, as if He said: "He did not attempt the steep path, nor did he believe."

Al-Mubarrad and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "*lā*" here means "*lam*": that is, "he did not attempt the steep path." Something similar is reported from Mujahid, and so repetition is not needed. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"He had folded his side over a hidden thing, so he neither revealed it nor advanced [it]."

That is, "he did not reveal it and did not advance." It was also said it runs in the manner of supplication, like their saying "*lā najāʾ*" (no deliverance).

Abu Zayd and a group of exegetes said: the meaning of the speech here is the interrogative in the sense of denial, its estimate being: "Why did he not attempt the steep path?" or "Would that he had attempted the steep path!"

Then God, glorified is He, explained the steep path, and said: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾, that is, what will inform you of its attempt?

﴿It is the freeing of a neck﴾: that is, it is freeing a slave and rescuing him from the captivity of slavery. Everything you release, you have untied; from it come "*fakk al-rahn*" (redeeming a pledge) and "*fakk al-kitāb*" (unsealing a letter). God, glorified is He, has made clear that the steep path is these acts of nearness mentioned, by which salvation from the Fire is achieved.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is a severe steep path in the Fire, before the Bridge, so attempt it through obedience to God.

Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: it is the Path (*al-Ṣirāṭ*) which is laid over Hell, sharp like the edge of a sword.

Kaʿb said: it is a fire before the Bridge.

It has also been said that there is an omission in the speech: that is, "And what will make you know what the attempting of the steep path is?" Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir and al-Kisaʾi read *fakka raqabatan* as a past verb with *raqabatan* in the accusative as its object, and likewise they read *aṭʿama* as a past verb. The rest read *fakku* or *iṭʿāmun* as verbal nouns (*maṣdar*), and the genitive *raqabatin* by the construct of the verbal noun to it. On the first reading, the two verbs are a substitute for "*iqtaḥama*" or an explanation of it, as if it were said: "He neither freed nor fed." *Al-fakk* originally means untying the fetter; manumission is called "*fakk*" because slavery is like a fetter, and the slave is called "*raqabah*" (neck) because by slavery he is like a captive tied by the neck.

﴿Or feeding on a day of hunger﴾. *Al-masghabah* is famine; *al-saghab* is hunger; *al-sāghib* is the hungry one.

Al-Raghib said: it is said of him: "*saghiba al-rajul saghaban wa-sughūban*," so he is "*sāghib*" and "*saghbān*," and *al-maṣghabah* is a noun of place derived from it. Abu ʿUbaydah recited:

"If you were free, O son of Qays ibn ʿAsim, you would not spend the night sated while your neighbour is hungry."

Al-Nakhaʿi said: ﴿on a day of hunger﴾ means a day in which food is scarce.

﴿An orphan of near relationship﴾: that is, of kinship. It is said: "So-and-so is my near relative and my close kin (*maqrabah*)." The orphan (*yatīm*) originally means the weak; it is said "*yatima al-rajul*" when he became weak. Among the people of language, the orphan is one who has no father; it has been said he is one who has neither father nor mother. From it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Mulawwah:

"To God I complain of the loss of Layla, as an orphan complains to God of the loss of his parents."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 90, verses 1–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Or a needy person in the dust﴾: that is, one who has nothing, as if he were stuck to the dust because of his poverty, and has no shelter but the dust. It is said: "al-rajul taraba yatrabu taraban wa matrabatan" (the man became destitute), when he became so poor that he was stuck to the dust in misery.

Mujahid said: "He is the one whom no clothing or anything else protects from the dust."

Qatadah said: "He is the one with a large family."

Ikrimah said: "He is the one in debt."

Abu Sinan said: "He is the one with a disability."

Ibn Jubayr said: "He is the one who has no one."

Ikrimah also said: "He is the one far from his homeland (turbah) and a stranger to his country." The first (view) is the more preferable, and from it is the verse of the Hudhali poet:

"And when a guest came to our land, we would spill the blood of camels in the dust of the stranger (al-hal)."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿dhi masghabatin﴾ as an attribute of "yawm" (day), and "yatiman" (an orphan) is the object of "ith'am" (feeding). Al-Hasan read "dha masghabatin" in the accusative as the object of "ith'am", meaning: they feed the one in hunger, and "yatiman" is a substitute (badal) for it.

﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon what is negated by "la" (not). "Thumma" (then) is used to indicate the delay in the rank of faith and the elevation of its station.

In this there is evidence that these acts of devotion benefit only together with faith. It was also said that the meaning is: then he was among those who believed that this was beneficial for them.

It was also said that the meaning is: he performed these acts of devotion for the sake of Allah, and "wa tawasaw" (and they enjoined one another) is conjoined to "amanu" (they believed): that is, some of them enjoined others to be patient in obeying Allah and in refraining from His disobedience, and patient over the trials and calamities that befell them. ﴿And enjoined one another to compassion﴾: that is, to mercy upon the servants of Allah. For when they did this, they showed mercy to the orphan and the needy, and they increased in doing good through charity and the like.

The indication by His words ﴿Those﴾ refers to the relative (al-mawsul) in view of its description by the attributes mentioned: they are the companions of the right hand (ashab al-maymanah), that is, the people of the right side, or the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), or those who will be given their books in their right hands. It has been said other than this, which we have already mentioned in surah al-Waqi'ah.

﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs﴾: that is, in the Qur'an, or in what is more general than it, so that the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanzilIyyah) and the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah), which indicate the Creator, Glorified is He, are included. ﴿They are the companions of the left hand (al-mash'amah)﴾: that is, the companions of the left side, or the companions of misfortune (ashab al-shu'm), or those who will be given their books in their left hands, or other than that which has preceded.

﴿Upon them is a fire, closed in﴾: that is, sealed shut and locked, from "asadtu al-bab" and "awsadtuhu": when I locked the door and closed it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"My she-camel longs for the mountains of Makkah, while between her and them are the gates of San'a, closed."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "muwsadah" with a waw. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Hafs read it with a hamzah in place of the waw, and both are dialects with the same meaning.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾ that he said: it is Makkah. ﴿And you are a lawful one (hill) in this city﴾: meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), for Allah made lawful to him on the day he entered Makkah that he could kill whom he wished and spare whom he wished. So on that day he executed Ibn Khatal by sabr (killing him while bound), while he was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah. After the Prophet (ﷺ), it was not lawful for anyone among the people to do in it any forbidden thing that Allah had forbidden. Thus Allah made lawful what he did to the people of Makkah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him concerning His words ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾, he said: Makkah. ﴿And you are a lawful one in this city﴾, he said: you, O Muhammad, it is lawful for you to fight in it, but not for anyone else.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Barzah al-Aslami who said: this verse was revealed: ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾, he said: it was made lawful for him to do in it whatever he wished. ﴿And a father and what he begot﴾, he said: by the father he means Adam, and by what he begot, his offspring.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning the verse, he said: "the father" is the one who begets, and "what he begot" is the barren one who does not beget, among men and women.

Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani also reported from him, likewise, ﴿and a father﴾, he said: it is Adam. ﴿Certainly We created man in toil (kabad)﴾, he said: in uprightness and erectness.

Ibn Jarir reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: in hardship (nasab).

Ibn Jarir reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: in difficulty.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: in the difficulty of his creation at birth, the growth of his teeth, his livelihood, and his circumcision.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: Allah created every thing that walks on four legs, except man, for he was created upright.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: upright in the womb of his mother, that an angel is assigned to him, and when the mother sleeps or lies down, he raises his head; otherwise he would drown in the blood.

Ibn Jarir reported from him also, concerning His words ﴿wealth piled up (lubada)﴾, he said: abundant.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih (authentic), reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿And We guided him to the two paths (al-najdayn)﴾, he said: the path of good and evil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾, he said: guidance and misguidance.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him, he said: the path of good and evil.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the chain of Sinan ibn Sa'd from Anas, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They are two paths; so the path of evil was not made more beloved to you than the path of good." Sinan ibn Sa'd alone transmitted it, and it is said: Sa'd ibn Sinan.

Yahya ibn Ma'in declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and al-Jawzajani said: munkar al-hadith (one whose narrations are rejected).

Ahmad said: I abandoned his hadith because of its confusion (idtirab). He narrated fifteen munkar (rejected) hadiths, none of which I recognize, and his hadith resembles the hadith of al-Hasan al-Basri, not the hadith of Anas.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through several chains from al-Hasan who said: it was mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say, and then he mentioned it.

This is mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), and Qatadah similarly transmitted it as mursal.

Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him, and what al-Tabarani transmitted from Umamah supports it: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O people, they are two paths: the path of good and the path of evil, so the path of evil was not made more beloved to you than the path of good." It is also supported by what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "They are only two paths: the path of good and the path of evil, so let the path of evil not be more beloved to you than the path of good."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾, he said: the two breasts.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Umar concerning His words ﴿But he has not attempted the steep ascent (al-'aqabah)﴾, he said: a mountain of cool water in Hell.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: al-'Aqabah is the Fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from him who said: al-'Aqabah is between Paradise and the Fire.

Al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from 'A'ishah who said: "When ﴿But he has not attempted the steep ascent﴾ was revealed, it was said: O Messenger of Allah, none of us has anything to free a slave, except that one of us has a black slave-girl who serves him. So if we ordered them to commit fornication and they bore children, we could free the children." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That I should be pleased with a whip in the cause of Allah is dearer to me than that I should order fornication and then free the child."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from her with the wording: "The reward of a whip's lash in the cause of Allah is greater than this."

The encouragement to free slaves is established in many hadiths. Among them, in the Two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever frees a believing slave, Allah will free from the Fire, for every limb of his, a limb of his, even the private part for the private part."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿on a day of hunger (masghabah)﴾, he said: famine.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿on a day of hunger﴾, he said: hunger.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also ﴿an orphan near of kin (dha maqrabah)﴾, he said: one of kinship. And concerning His words ﴿one in the dust (dha matrabah)﴾, he said: one far from the dust, that is, a stranger far from his homeland.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, reported from him also ﴿Or a needy person in the dust﴾, he said: he is the one cast aside who has no house.

In another wording from al-Hakim: he is the one whom nothing protects from the dust.

In another wording: he is the one clinging to the dust because of the severity of his poverty.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, "from the Prophet (ﷺ)", concerning ﴿a needy person in the dust﴾, he said: the one whose shelter is the garbage heaps.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and enjoined one another to compassion﴾, that by it he means the mercy of all people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿muwsadah﴾, he said: its doors are locked.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah concerning ﴿muwsadah﴾, he said: sealed shut.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 90, verses 1–20 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan (*makkiyyah*) without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah ﴿I swear by this city﴾ was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar to this.

[p. 1623]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying "*Lā uqsimu*" (I do not swear): the "*lā*" is superfluous (*zāʾidah*), and the meaning is "I swear by this city." The discussion of this has already passed in the commentary on ﴿I do not swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾. Among the uses of the superfluous "*lā*" in speech other than an oath is the saying of the poet:

"I remembered Layla, and passion (*ṣabābah*) overcame me, and the core of the heart nearly splits, [not] splitting."

That is, "it splits." Among the same usage is His saying: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 12], meaning "that you prostrate."

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes (*mufassirūn*) have agreed that this is an oath by the sacred city, which is Mecca.

Al-Jumhur read "*Lā uqsimu*," while al-Hasan and al-Aʿmash read "*La-uqsimu*" without an alif. It has been said that it is a negation of the oath, and the meaning is: I do not swear by this city if you are not in it after your departure from it.

Mujahid said: "*lā*" is a rebuttal (*radd*) of those who denied the resurrection (*baʿth*), then he began and said "uqsimu" (I swear). The meaning is: the matter is not as you suppose. The first view is preferable.

The meaning is: I swear by the sacred city in which you are a lawful resident (*ḥill*).

Al-Wasiti said that the intended "city" is Medina. Apart from its being contrary to the consensus of the exegetes, this is also refuted by the surah being Meccan and not Medinan.

The clause "*wa-anta ḥillun bi-hādhā al-balad*" (and you are a lawful resident in this city) is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍ*), and the meaning is: I swear by this city, ﴿and by the begetter and what he begot. Certainly We created man in toil﴾. It is interposed between them with this clause, and the meaning is: among the hardships is that one like you, despite the great sanctity of this city, is made lawful in it, just as game is made lawful outside the sanctuary (*ḥaram*).

Al-Wahidi said: *al-ḥill*, *al-ḥalāl* and *al-maḥall* are one and the same; it is the opposite of the forbidden (*al-muḥarram*). God made Mecca lawful for His Prophet ﷺ on the day of the Conquest until he fought in it, and the Prophet ﷺ had said: "It was not made lawful for anyone before me, nor will it be made lawful for anyone after me, and it was made lawful for me only for an hour of a day." He said: The meaning is that when God mentioned the oath by Mecca, this indicated the greatness of its status despite its being sacred, so He promised His Prophet ﷺ that He would make it lawful for him so that he would fight in it and conquer it at his hand. This is a promise from God, the Exalted, that He would make it lawful for him so that it would be lawful for him. End of quotation.

So the meaning is: "and you are a lawful resident in this city in the future," as in His saying: ﴿Indeed you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30]. Mujahid said: the meaning is, whatever you do in it, you are lawful (*fa-anta ḥill*).

Qatadah said: "You are lawful in it" means you are not sinful: that is, you do not commit in this city what is forbidden for you to commit, unlike the polytheists who commit disbelief and sins in it.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "I do not swear by this city" while you are residing in it and it is your dwelling place. According to the view that "*lā*" is a negation and not superfluous, the meaning is: I do not swear by it while you are residing in it, so you are more worthy of the oath by you. According to the view that it is superfluous, the meaning is: I swear by this city in which you reside, as an honour for you and an exaltation of your rank, because by your residence in it, it has become great and noble, and has increased in the nobility and greatness it already had. However, this is established in the language of the Arabs: the word *ḥill* comes in the sense of *ḥāll* (resident). And just as the clause may be parenthetical, it may also be in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). ﴿And begetter and what he begot﴾ is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to "the city."

Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Abu Salih said: ﴿and begetter﴾ means Adam, ﴿and what he begot﴾ means whatever was propagated from his offspring. He swore by them because they are the most wondrous of what God created on the face of the earth, due to what is in them of eloquence, intellect and management, and among them are the prophets, scholars and righteous.

Abu ʿImran al-Jawni said: the begetter is Abraham, and "what he begot" is his descendants.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "*mā*" is an expression for people, like His saying: ﴿what seems good to you﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 3]. It has been said: the begetter is Abraham, and the begotten is Ishmael and Muhammad ﷺ.

ʿIkrimah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: ﴿and begetter﴾ means the one who fathers (*alladhī yūlad lahu*), and ﴿and what he begot﴾ means the barren one who does not beget. It seems that these two took "*mā*" as a negation, and this is far-fetched; it is only valid by supposing an omitted relative pronoun: that is, "and the begetter and the one who did not beget," and the omission of a relative pronoun is not permitted according to the Basrans.

ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi said: it is general for every begetter and begotten among all animals, and Ibn Jarir chose this view.

﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾: this is the answer to the oath. "Man" (*al-insān*) is this human species. "*Al-kabad*" is hardship and difficulty. It is said: "*kābadtu al-amr*" (I struggled with the matter): I endured its hardship. Man continues to struggle with this world and endure its hardships until he dies. The root meaning of *kabad* is hardship, and from it comes "*takabbada al-laban*" (the milk thickened and became firm) when it becomes thick and firm. It is also said "*kabida al-rajul*" when his liver was afflicted, then it came to be used for every hardship and difficulty. From it is the saying of Abu al-Asbagh:

"I have a cousin who, if all people were in toil, would remain confined by arrows, shooting at me."

Al-Hasan said: he struggles with the calamities of this world and the hardships of the Hereafter.

He also said: he struggles with gratitude in times of ease, and he struggles with patience in times of hardship; he is never free of one of them.

Al-Kalbi said: this verse was revealed concerning a man of the Banu Jumah called Abu al-Ashaddayn, who used to take a leather hide of ʿUkaz and place it under his feet, saying: "Whoever removes me from it, for him is such-and-such." Ten men would pull it until it tore, yet his feet would not move. He was one of the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ, and concerning him was revealed ﴿Does he suppose that no one will have power over him﴾, meaning because of his strength. On this view, the meaning of ﴿in toil﴾ is: in the hardness of creation. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿in toil﴾ is that he is bold of heart and hard of liver. ﴿Does he suppose that no one will have power over him﴾: that is, does the son of Adam suppose that no one will have power over him and no one will take vengeance upon him? Or does Abu al-Ashaddayn suppose that no one will have power over him? "*Anna*" here is the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, and its noun is an implied pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr shaʾn*).

Then He, glorified is He, informed about the speech of this man, and said: ﴿He says: I have squandered abundant wealth﴾, that is, much accumulated wealth, some of it piled upon some.

Al-Layth said: *mālun lubad* is wealth whose ending is not feared because of its abundance.

[p. 1624]

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: he says, "I have squandered much wealth in hostility to Muhammad."

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn ʿAmir ibn Nawfal, who committed a sin and sought a ruling from the Prophet ﷺ, and he ordered him to make expiation, and he said: "My wealth has gone in expiations and expenditures since I entered the religion of Muhammad."

Al-Jumhur read *lubbadan* with a damma on the lam, a fatha on the ba, and shadda.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: *lubad* is on the pattern *fuʿal* from *al-talbīd* (layering), which is abundant wealth piled upon itself.

Al-Zajjaj said: *fuʿal* indicates abundance; it is said "*rajulun ḥuṭam*" when he is one who breaks much.

Al-Farrāʾ said: its singular is *lubadah* and the plural is *lubad*.

The explanation of this has already passed in the surah of the Jinn.

﴿Does he suppose that no one has seen him?﴾ That is, does he suppose that no one has witnessed him? Qatadah said: Does he suppose that God, glorified is He, has not seen him, and will not ask him about his wealth, from where he earned it and where he spent it? Al-Kalbi said: he was lying, he did not spend what he claimed; so God said: Does he suppose that God did not see that from him, whether he did it or did not do it, whether he spent or did not spend?

Then He mentioned what He had bestowed upon them, so that they might take heed, and said: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes﴾, with which he sees.

And a tongue with which he speaks, and two lips with which he covers his mouth.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: did We not do to him what indicates that God is capable of resurrecting him? The *shafah* (lip) has a missing *lām*, and its original form is *shafahah*, as evidenced by its diminutive *shufayhah*.

﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾. *Al-najd* is the road in an elevated place.

The exegetes said: We made clear to him the path of good and the path of evil.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: Did We not make him know the path of good and the path of evil, both made clear, like the two high roads being clear?

ʿIkrimah, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak said: *al-najdān* are the two breasts, because they are like the two paths for the life and sustenance of the child. The first view is preferable.

The root meaning of *najd* is an elevated place, its plural is *nujūd*, and from it Najd was named because of its elevation above the lowland of Tihamah. So *al-najdān* are the two high roads. From it is the saying of Imru al-Qays:

"A group of them cut through the valley of Nakhlah, and another group of them cut through the highland of Kabkab."

﴿But he did not attempt the steep path﴾. *Al-iqtiḥām* is throwing oneself into something without deliberation. It is said from it: "*qaḥama fī al-amr quḥūman*," that is, he threw himself into it without deliberation. And "*taqḥīm al-nafs fī al-shayʾ*" is putting oneself into it without deliberation. *Al-quḥmah* with a damma is ruin.

*Al-ʿaqabah* originally means the road in a mountain, named so because of the difficulty of traversing it. It is a parable that God, glorified is He, struck for striving against the self, desire and Satan in works of righteousness, making him like one who laboriously climbs the steep path.

Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjaj said: God mentioned here "*lā*" only once, and the Arabs hardly ever use "*lā*" alone with the past verb in such a position unless they repeat it in another utterance, as in His saying: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 31]. He used it singly here to indicate the meaning through the end of the speech. So His saying ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ may stand in place of repetition, as if He said: "He did not attempt the steep path, nor did he believe."

Al-Mubarrad and Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: "*lā*" here means "*lam*": that is, "he did not attempt the steep path." Something similar is reported from Mujahid, and so repetition is not needed. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"He had folded his side over a hidden thing, so he neither revealed it nor advanced [it]."

That is, "he did not reveal it and did not advance." It was also said it runs in the manner of supplication, like their saying "*lā najāʾ*" (no deliverance).

Abu Zayd and a group of exegetes said: the meaning of the speech here is the interrogative in the sense of denial, its estimate being: "Why did he not attempt the steep path?" or "Would that he had attempted the steep path!"

Then God, glorified is He, explained the steep path, and said: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep path is?﴾, that is, what will inform you of its attempt?

﴿It is the freeing of a neck﴾: that is, it is freeing a slave and rescuing him from the captivity of slavery. Everything you release, you have untied; from it come "*fakk al-rahn*" (redeeming a pledge) and "*fakk al-kitāb*" (unsealing a letter). God, glorified is He, has made clear that the steep path is these acts of nearness mentioned, by which salvation from the Fire is achieved.

Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is a severe steep path in the Fire, before the Bridge, so attempt it through obedience to God.

Mujahid, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: it is the Path (*al-Ṣirāṭ*) which is laid over Hell, sharp like the edge of a sword.

Kaʿb said: it is a fire before the Bridge.

It has also been said that there is an omission in the speech: that is, "And what will make you know what the attempting of the steep path is?" Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir and al-Kisaʾi read *fakka raqabatan* as a past verb with *raqabatan* in the accusative as its object, and likewise they read *aṭʿama* as a past verb. The rest read *fakku* or *iṭʿāmun* as verbal nouns (*maṣdar*), and the genitive *raqabatin* by the construct of the verbal noun to it. On the first reading, the two verbs are a substitute for "*iqtaḥama*" or an explanation of it, as if it were said: "He neither freed nor fed." *Al-fakk* originally means untying the fetter; manumission is called "*fakk*" because slavery is like a fetter, and the slave is called "*raqabah*" (neck) because by slavery he is like a captive tied by the neck.

﴿Or feeding on a day of hunger﴾. *Al-masghabah* is famine; *al-saghab* is hunger; *al-sāghib* is the hungry one.

Al-Raghib said: it is said of him: "*saghiba al-rajul saghaban wa-sughūban*," so he is "*sāghib*" and "*saghbān*," and *al-maṣghabah* is a noun of place derived from it. Abu ʿUbaydah recited:

"If you were free, O son of Qays ibn ʿAsim, you would not spend the night sated while your neighbour is hungry."

Al-Nakhaʿi said: ﴿on a day of hunger﴾ means a day in which food is scarce.

﴿An orphan of near relationship﴾: that is, of kinship. It is said: "So-and-so is my near relative and my close kin (*maqrabah*)." The orphan (*yatīm*) originally means the weak; it is said "*yatima al-rajul*" when he became weak. Among the people of language, the orphan is one who has no father; it has been said he is one who has neither father nor mother. From it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Mulawwah:

"To God I complain of the loss of Layla, as an orphan complains to God of the loss of his parents."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 90, verses 1–20 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Or a needy person in the dust﴾: that is, one who has nothing, as if he were stuck to the dust because of his poverty, and has no shelter but the dust. It is said: "al-rajul taraba yatrabu taraban wa matrabatan" (the man became destitute), when he became so poor that he was stuck to the dust in misery.

Mujahid said: "He is the one whom no clothing or anything else protects from the dust."

Qatadah said: "He is the one with a large family."

Ikrimah said: "He is the one in debt."

Abu Sinan said: "He is the one with a disability."

Ibn Jubayr said: "He is the one who has no one."

Ikrimah also said: "He is the one far from his homeland (turbah) and a stranger to his country." The first (view) is the more preferable, and from it is the verse of the Hudhali poet:

"And when a guest came to our land, we would spill the blood of camels in the dust of the stranger (al-hal)."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿dhi masghabatin﴾ as an attribute of "yawm" (day), and "yatiman" (an orphan) is the object of "ith'am" (feeding). Al-Hasan read "dha masghabatin" in the accusative as the object of "ith'am", meaning: they feed the one in hunger, and "yatiman" is a substitute (badal) for it.

﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon what is negated by "la" (not). "Thumma" (then) is used to indicate the delay in the rank of faith and the elevation of its station.

In this there is evidence that these acts of devotion benefit only together with faith. It was also said that the meaning is: then he was among those who believed that this was beneficial for them.

It was also said that the meaning is: he performed these acts of devotion for the sake of Allah, and "wa tawasaw" (and they enjoined one another) is conjoined to "amanu" (they believed): that is, some of them enjoined others to be patient in obeying Allah and in refraining from His disobedience, and patient over the trials and calamities that befell them. ﴿And enjoined one another to compassion﴾: that is, to mercy upon the servants of Allah. For when they did this, they showed mercy to the orphan and the needy, and they increased in doing good through charity and the like.

The indication by His words ﴿Those﴾ refers to the relative (al-mawsul) in view of its description by the attributes mentioned: they are the companions of the right hand (ashab al-maymanah), that is, the people of the right side, or the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), or those who will be given their books in their right hands. It has been said other than this, which we have already mentioned in surah al-Waqi'ah.

﴿And those who disbelieved in Our signs﴾: that is, in the Qur'an, or in what is more general than it, so that the revealed signs (al-ayat al-tanzilIyyah) and the created signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah), which indicate the Creator, Glorified is He, are included. ﴿They are the companions of the left hand (al-mash'amah)﴾: that is, the companions of the left side, or the companions of misfortune (ashab al-shu'm), or those who will be given their books in their left hands, or other than that which has preceded.

﴿Upon them is a fire, closed in﴾: that is, sealed shut and locked, from "asadtu al-bab" and "awsadtuhu": when I locked the door and closed it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"My she-camel longs for the mountains of Makkah, while between her and them are the gates of San'a, closed."

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "muwsadah" with a waw. Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Hafs read it with a hamzah in place of the waw, and both are dialects with the same meaning.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾ that he said: it is Makkah. ﴿And you are a lawful one (hill) in this city﴾: meaning the Prophet (ﷺ), for Allah made lawful to him on the day he entered Makkah that he could kill whom he wished and spare whom he wished. So on that day he executed Ibn Khatal by sabr (killing him while bound), while he was clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah. After the Prophet (ﷺ), it was not lawful for anyone among the people to do in it any forbidden thing that Allah had forbidden. Thus Allah made lawful what he did to the people of Makkah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from him concerning His words ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾, he said: Makkah. ﴿And you are a lawful one in this city﴾, he said: you, O Muhammad, it is lawful for you to fight in it, but not for anyone else.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Barzah al-Aslami who said: this verse was revealed: ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾, he said: it was made lawful for him to do in it whatever he wished. ﴿And a father and what he begot﴾, he said: by the father he means Adam, and by what he begot, his offspring.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning the verse, he said: "the father" is the one who begets, and "what he begot" is the barren one who does not beget, among men and women.

Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani also reported from him, likewise, ﴿and a father﴾, he said: it is Adam. ﴿Certainly We created man in toil (kabad)﴾, he said: in uprightness and erectness.

Ibn Jarir reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: in hardship (nasab).

Ibn Jarir reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: in difficulty.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: in the difficulty of his creation at birth, the growth of his teeth, his livelihood, and his circumcision.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: Allah created every thing that walks on four legs, except man, for he was created upright.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azamah reported from him also: ﴿Certainly We created man in toil﴾, he said: upright in the womb of his mother, that an angel is assigned to him, and when the mother sleeps or lies down, he raises his head; otherwise he would drown in the blood.

Ibn Jarir reported from him also, concerning His words ﴿wealth piled up (lubada)﴾, he said: abundant.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih (authentic), reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His words ﴿And We guided him to the two paths (al-najdayn)﴾, he said: the path of good and evil.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾, he said: guidance and misguidance.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him, he said: the path of good and evil.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the chain of Sinan ibn Sa'd from Anas, who said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They are two paths; so the path of evil was not made more beloved to you than the path of good." Sinan ibn Sa'd alone transmitted it, and it is said: Sa'd ibn Sinan.

Yahya ibn Ma'in declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and al-Jawzajani said: munkar al-hadith (one whose narrations are rejected).

Ahmad said: I abandoned his hadith because of its confusion (idtirab). He narrated fifteen munkar (rejected) hadiths, none of which I recognize, and his hadith resembles the hadith of al-Hasan al-Basri, not the hadith of Anas.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through several chains from al-Hasan who said: it was mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say, and then he mentioned it.

This is mursal (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain), and Qatadah similarly transmitted it as mursal.

Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him, and what al-Tabarani transmitted from Umamah supports it: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O people, they are two paths: the path of good and the path of evil, so the path of evil was not made more beloved to you than the path of good." It is also supported by what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "They are only two paths: the path of good and the path of evil, so let the path of evil not be more beloved to you than the path of good."

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾, he said: the two breasts.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Umar concerning His words ﴿But he has not attempted the steep ascent (al-'aqabah)﴾, he said: a mountain of cool water in Hell.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: al-'Aqabah is the Fire.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from him who said: al-'Aqabah is between Paradise and the Fire.

Al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from 'A'ishah who said: "When ﴿But he has not attempted the steep ascent﴾ was revealed, it was said: O Messenger of Allah, none of us has anything to free a slave, except that one of us has a black slave-girl who serves him. So if we ordered them to commit fornication and they bore children, we could free the children." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "That I should be pleased with a whip in the cause of Allah is dearer to me than that I should order fornication and then free the child."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from her with the wording: "The reward of a whip's lash in the cause of Allah is greater than this."

The encouragement to free slaves is established in many hadiths. Among them, in the Two Sahihs and others, from Abu Hurayrah who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever frees a believing slave, Allah will free from the Fire, for every limb of his, a limb of his, even the private part for the private part."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿on a day of hunger (masghabah)﴾, he said: famine.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿on a day of hunger﴾, he said: hunger.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also ﴿an orphan near of kin (dha maqrabah)﴾, he said: one of kinship. And concerning His words ﴿one in the dust (dha matrabah)﴾, he said: one far from the dust, that is, a stranger far from his homeland.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, reported from him also ﴿Or a needy person in the dust﴾, he said: he is the one cast aside who has no house.

In another wording from al-Hakim: he is the one whom nothing protects from the dust.

In another wording: he is the one clinging to the dust because of the severity of his poverty.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Umar, "from the Prophet (ﷺ)", concerning ﴿a needy person in the dust﴾, he said: the one whose shelter is the garbage heaps.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and enjoined one another to compassion﴾, that by it he means the mercy of all people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿muwsadah﴾, he said: its doors are locked.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah concerning ﴿muwsadah﴾, he said: sealed shut.
